title: Everyone who thirsts (Isaiah 55:1–11)
hook: come, buy without money; my word shall not return empty

segments.voice: Yesterday, the suffering servant, and your line was by his stripes. Whose load did you lighten? Day four hundred seventy-one.

Picture a market in an ancient city. Stalls of bread and dates, sacks of grain, jars of wine, goat's milk in skins. And the sellers shouting over each other, the way they still do in markets around the world: over here, best price, come and buy. Now one voice cuts through the noise with an offer nobody else is making. Come and buy, it says. But you don't need money. Bring nothing. Take wine and milk anyway. Free. In a market, that sounds either like a trick or like madness. Isaiah puts it in God's mouth. Today, the strangest sales pitch in the Bible.
screen: `AN ANCIENT MARKET.` → `EVERY SELLER SHOUTING.` → `ONE VOICE: BRING NO MONEY.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the King James Bible: "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price." Ho is a market cry. Hey! Over here! Water, then wine and milk: from what keeps you alive to what makes a feast. And the price is nothing. Then God asks a question that feels written for our own time: "Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not?" Why spend your paycheck, your hours, your attention, on things that don't fill you? Listen, God says, and eat what is good. The chapter goes on: seek the Lord while he may be found. And then a line people quote when nothing makes sense: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD." As high as the heavens are above the earth. Then a picture from farming. Rain and snow fall from the sky, and they don't go back up empty. They water the earth, make it sprout, give seed to the sower and bread to the eater. "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void." God's word, like rain, does its work, even when you can't see it yet. And the chapter ends in a burst: the mountains and hills break into singing, and all the trees of the field clap their hands. Christians hear in this chapter the free gift they call grace, offered to everyone. Jewish readers hear God's covenant love, offered again to exiles on their way home.
screen: `HO! A MARKET CRY.` · `WHY SPEND ON WHAT ISN'T BREAD?` · `MY WAYS ARE NOT YOUR WAYS.` · `THE WORD RETURNS NOT VOID.` · then, large: `WITHOUT MONEY AND WITHOUT PRICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what you've been spending on that isn't bread. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day: where did your money go, your time, your attention? Without judging, notice one thing that didn't fill you. Then notice one thing that did, and that cost nothing: a meal with someone, a walk, a moment of quiet, a laugh. Hold that one. Then think of something you could give away today the same way, freely, without price: time, help, a skill, a meal. If you pray, you can give thanks for what came free. The bell holds the time.
Everyone who thirsts. Isaiah's market cry: come to the waters, buy wine and milk with no money at all, free to all who are thirsty.
Your line: without money, without price. Today, give one thing freely, with no payback expected: your time, your help, a meal, a skill, a ride. Day four hundred seventy-one.

screen: `DAY 471 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: GOOD NEWS TO THE POOR.`

howItsDone: Isaiah 55 is read at the Easter Vigil in Catholic and many Anglican and Lutheran churches, and Protestant preachers often use its opening as an invitation to grace; verse 8 is often turned to in times of confusion or loss.

fork.setup: you're in the market with no money, thirsty and hungry. a voice shouts, come, buy wine and milk. what's the catch?
options: there is none: without money and without price.
you must prove you deserve it first.
fork.reveal: "come, buy wine and milk without money and without price." the strangest sales pitch in the Bible: it's free.

original.note: Hebrew: ho, everyone who thirsts! a market cry.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poetic way of saying God is generous.
what it means: a market cry offering food and drink for nothing, and a word that, like rain, always does its work.
what a scholar hears: hoy, an attention cry also used in laments. the chapter closes Second Isaiah's poems, ending with a covenant offered to all and the trees clapping.
